danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 27
paragraphs: Franskmændenes udbredelse i Moskva, der strålede stjerneformet ud, nåede først om aftenen den anden september den bydel, hvor Pierre opholdt sig.

Efter de sidste to dage tilbragt i ensomhed og usædvanlige omstændigheder var Pierre i en tilstand, der grænsede til vanvid. Han var fuldstændig besat af én vedholdende tanke. Han vidste ikke, hvordan eller hvornår denne tanke havde grebet ham, men han huskede intet af fortiden, forstod intet af nutiden, og alt, hvad han så og hørte, forekom ham som en drøm.

Han havde forladt sit hjem blot for at undslippe det indviklede net af livets krav, der omspændte ham, og som han i sin nuværende tilstand var ude af stand til at rede ud. Han var taget til Josef Aleksejevitjs hus under påskud af at sortere den afdødes bøger og papirer, kun i søgen efter hvile fra livets tummel, for i hans erindring var Josef Aleksejevitj forbundet med en verden af evige, højtidelige og rolige tanker, ganske modsat den urolige forvirring, han følte sig draget ind i. Da han sad med albuerne på det støvede skrivebord i arbejdsværelsets dødlignende stilhed, steg rolige og betydningsfulde minder fra de seneste dage et efter et op i hans fantasi, især fra slaget ved Borodino og den uklare fornemmelse af sin egen ubetydelighed og upålidelighed sammenlignet med sandheden, enkelheden og styrken hos den klasse mennesker, han i tankerne betegnede som dem. Da Gerasim vækkede ham af hans drømmeri, faldt det ham ind at deltage i det folkelige forsvar af Moskva, som han vidste var planlagt. Med det mål for øje havde han bedt Gerasim om at skaffe ham en bondefrakke og en pistol og havde betroet ham sine planer om at forblive i Josef Aleksejevitjs hus og holde sit navn hemmeligt. Derefter, under den første dag tilbragt i uvirksomhed og ensomhed (han forsøgte adskillige gange at fæstne sin opmærksomhed ved frimurermanuskripterne, men var ude af stand til det), dukkede den idé, der tidligere var faldet ham ind, om den kabbalistiske sammenhæng mellem hans navn og Bonapartes, atter og atter vagt op for ham. Men idéen om, at han, L'russe Besuhof, var bestemt til at sætte en grænse for Udyrets magt, var endnu blot en af de griller, der ofte gik gennem hans hoved og ikke efterlod noget spor.

Da Pierre, der havde købt frakken udelukkende med det formål at deltage blandt folket i forsvaret af Moskva, mødte Rostov-familien, og Natasja havde sagt til ham: »Bliver De i Moskva?... Hvor storslået!« blinkede tanken op i hans sind, at det virkelig ville være godt, selv om Moskva blev taget, for ham at forblive dér og gøre det, han var forudbestemt til.

Næste dag, med den ene tanke ikke at skåne sig selv og på ingen måde at halte bagefter dem, gik Pierre ud til Trehjøjsporten. Men da han vendte tilbage til huset, overbevist om at Moskva ikke ville blive forsvaret, følte han pludselig, at det, der før havde forekommet ham blot en mulighed, nu var blevet absolut nødvendigt og uundgåeligt. Han måtte forblive i Moskva, skjule sit navn og møde Napoleon og dræbe ham og enten gå til grunde eller gøre en ende på hele Europas elendighed — som det forekom ham udelukkende skyldtes Napoleon.

Pierre kendte alle detaljer om det forsøg på Bonapartes liv i 1809 udført af en tysk student i Wien og vidste, at studenten var blevet skudt. Og den risiko, han ville udsætte sit liv for ved at gennemføre sin plan, ophidsede ham endnu mere.

To lige stærke følelser drog uimodståeligt Pierre mod dette mål. Den første var en følelse af nødvendigheden af ofring og lidelse i betragtning af den fælles ulykke, den samme følelse, der havde fået ham til at tage til Mozjajsk den femogtyvende og trænge sig helt ind i slagets tætteste tummel, og som nu havde fået ham til at flygte hjemmefra og i stedet for den luksus og komfort, han var vant til, at sove på en hård sofa uden at klæde sig af og spise den samme mad som Gerasim. Den anden var den vage og helt russiske følelse af foragt for alt konventionelt, kunstigt og menneskeligt — for alt det, som flertallet betragter som det højeste gode i verden. Pierre havde første gang oplevet denne mærkelige og fængslende følelse i Sloboda-paladset, da han pludselig havde følt, at rigdom, magt og livet selv — alt det, mennesker så omhyggeligt erhverver og bevogter — kun har nogen værdi i kraft af den glæde, hvormed det alt sammen kan opgives.

Det var den følelse, der får en frivillig rekrut til at bruge sin sidste øre på drikkeri, og en beruset mand til at smadre spejle eller glas uden synlig grund og vel vidende, at det vil koste ham alle hans penge: den følelse, der får et menneske til at udføre handlinger, som fra et almindeligt synspunkt er vanvittige, for ligesom at prøve sin egen personlige kraft og styrke og bekræfte eksistensen af et højere, ikke-menneskeligt kriterium for livet.

Lige fra den dag Pierre for første gang oplevede denne følelse i Sloboda-paladset, havde han uafbrudt været under dens indflydelse, men først nu fandt han fuld tilfredsstillelse for den. Desuden blev Pierre i dette øjeblik støttet i sin plan og forhindret i at opgive den af det, han allerede havde gjort i den retning. Hvis han nu forlod Moskva ligesom alle andre, ville hans flugt hjemmefra, bondekappen, pistolen og hans erklæring til Rostov-familien om, at han ville forblive i Moskva, alt sammen blive ikke blot meningsløst, men foragteligt og latterligt, og det var Pierre meget følsom over for.

Pierres fysiske tilstand svarede som altid til hans mentale. Den uvante grove kost, den vodka, han drak i de dage, fraværet af vin og cigarer, hans snavsede, uskiftede linned, to næsten søvnløse nætter tilbragt på en kort sofa uden sengetøj — alt dette holdt ham i en ophidset tilstand, der grænsede til vanvid.

Klokken var to om eftermiddagen. Franskmændene var allerede rykket ind i Moskva. Pierre vidste det, men i stedet for at handle tænkte han kun på sit forehavende og gennemgik dets mindste detaljer i tankerne. I sin fantasi forestillede han sig hverken selve hugget eller Napoleons død tydeligt, men med usædvanlig livfuldhed og melankolsk nydelse forestillede han sig sin egen undergang og heroiske udholdenhed.

»Ja, alene, for alles skyld, må jeg gøre det eller gå til grunde!« tænkte han. »Ja, jeg vil nærme mig... og så pludselig... med pistol eller dolk? Men det er det samme! 'Det er ikke mig, men Forsynets hånd, der straffer dig,' vil jeg sige,« tænkte han og forestillede sig, hvad han ville sige, når han dræbte Napoleon. »Nå vel, tag mig og henret mig!« fortsatte han og talte til sig selv, mens han bøjede hovedet med et trist, men fast udtryk.

Mens Pierre, stående midt i værelset, talte med sig selv på denne måde, åbnedes arbejdsværelsets dør, og på tærsklen viste sig skikkelsen af Makar Aleksejevitj, altid så frygtsom før, men nu ganske forvandlet.

Hans slobrok var uknappet, hans ansigt rødt og forvrænget. Han var tydeligvis beruset. Da han fik øje på Pierre, blev han først forvirret, men da han bemærkede forlegenheden i Pierres ansigt, blev han straks modig og gik, vaklende på sine tynde ben, ind midt i værelset.
»De er bange,« sagde han fortroligt med hæs stemme. »Jeg siger, jeg overgiver mig ikke, siger jeg... Har jeg ikke ret, min herre?«
Han holdt inde og så så pludselig pistolen på bordet, greb den med uventet hurtighed og løb ud i gangen.

Gerasim og portieren, der var fulgt efter Makar Aleksejevitj, standsede ham i forstuen og forsøgte at tage pistolen fra ham. Pierre, der kom ud i gangen, kiggede med medlidenhed og afsky på den halvgale gamle mand. Makar Aleksejevitj, rynkende panden af anstrengelse, holdt fast i pistolen og skreg hæst, åbenbart med en heroisk indbildning i hovedet.
»Til angreb! Enter dem! Nej, I skal ikke få den,« skreg han.
»Nå, nu, vær venlig, nu. Vær så god — vær venlig, min herre, at give slip! Vær venlig, min herre...« bad Gerasim og forsøgte forsigtigt at styre Makar Aleksejevitj ved albuerne hen mod døren.
»Hvem er du? Bonaparte!...« skreg Makar Aleksejevitj.
»Det er ikke rigtigt, min herre. Kom nu ind på Deres værelse og hvil. Vær venlig at give mig pistolen.«
»Bort med dig, din usle træl! Rør mig ikke! Se dette?« skreg Makar Aleksejevitj og svingede pistolen. »Enter dem!«
»Grib fat!« hviskede Gerasim til portieren.
De greb Makar Aleksejevitj ved armene og trak ham hen til døren.
Forstuen fyldtes af den uharmoniske lyd af en kamp og en beruset, hæs stemme.
Pludselig genlød en ny lyd, et gennemtrængende kvindeskrig, fra trappen, og kogepigen kom løbende ind i forstuen.
»Det er dem! Du godeste Gud! Åh, Herre, fire af dem, ryttere!« råbte hun.
Gerasim og portieren slap Makar Aleksejevitj, og i den nu stille gang kunne lyden af adskillige hænder, der bankede på hoveddøren, høres.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: The spread of the French through Moscow, radiating outward like a star, only reached the quarter where Pierre was staying by the evening of September second.

After the last two days spent in solitude and unusual circumstances, Pierre was in a state bordering on insanity. He was completely obsessed by one persistent thought. He did not know how or when this thought had taken such possession of him, but he remembered nothing of the past, understood nothing of the present, and all he saw and heard seemed like a dream.

He had left home only to escape the complicated tangle of life's demands that enmeshed him, and which in his present condition he was unable to sort out. He had gone to Joseph Alexeevich's house on the pretext of organizing the deceased's books and papers, but really in search of rest from life's turmoil, for in his mind the memory of Joseph Alexeevich was connected with a world of eternal, solemn, and calm thoughts, quite opposite to the restless confusion into which he felt himself being drawn. He sought a quiet refuge, and in Joseph Alexeevich's study he really found it. When he sat with his elbows on the dusty writing table in the deathlike stillness of the study, calm and significant memories of the last few days rose one after another in his imagination, particularly the battle of Borodino and that vague sense of his own insignificance and insincerity compared with the truth, simplicity, and strength of the class of men he mentally classed as "they." When Gerasim roused him from his reverie, the idea occurred to him of taking part in the popular defense of Moscow, which he knew was being planned. With that aim he had asked Gerasim to get him a peasant's coat and a pistol, and had confided his intention of remaining in Joseph Alexeevich's house and keeping his name secret. Then during the first day spent in inaction and solitude (he tried several times to concentrate on the Masonic manuscripts but couldn't), the idea that had previously occurred to him of the cabalistic significance of his name in connection with Bonaparte's more than once vaguely presented itself. But the idea that he, L'russe Besuhof, was destined to set a limit to the power of the Beast was as yet only one of those fancies that often passed through his mind and left no trace.

When, having bought the coat merely to take part among the people in the defense of Moscow, Pierre had met the Rostovs and Natasha had said to him: "Are you remaining in Moscow?... How wonderful!" the thought flashed into his mind that it really would be a good thing, even if Moscow were taken, for him to remain there and do what he was predestined to do.

The next day, focused solely on not sparing himself and not lagging behind anyone, Pierre went to the Three Hills gate. But when he returned to the house, convinced that Moscow would not be defended, he suddenly felt that what had previously seemed merely a possibility had now become absolutely necessary and inevitable. He must remain in Moscow, conceal his name, meet Napoleon, and kill him—either perishing himself or putting an end to the misery of all Europe, which seemed to him entirely due to Napoleon.

Pierre knew all the details of the attempt on Bonaparte's life in 1809 by a German student in Vienna, and knew that the student had been shot. And the risk to which he would expose his own life by carrying out his plan excited him still more.

Two equally powerful feelings drew Pierre irresistibly to this purpose. The first was a feeling of the necessity of sacrifice and suffering in view of the common calamity—the same feeling that had caused him to go to Mozhaysk on the twenty-fifth and to plunge into the very thick of the battle, and had now caused him to run away from home and, in place of the luxury and comfort he was accustomed to, to sleep on a hard sofa without undressing and eat the same food as Gerasim. The other was that vague and distinctly Russian feeling of contempt for everything conventional, artificial, and human—for everything the majority of men regard as the greatest good in the world. Pierre had first experienced this strange and fascinating feeling at the Sloboda Palace, when he had suddenly felt that wealth, power, and life—all that men so painstakingly acquire and guard—if it has any worth, has so only by reason of the joy with which it can all be renounced.

It was the feeling that makes a volunteer recruit spend his last penny on drink, and a drunken man smash mirrors or glasses for no apparent reason, knowing it will cost him everything he owns: the feeling which causes a man to do things that from an ordinary point of view are insane, as if to test his personal power and strength, affirming the existence of a higher, nonhuman standard of life.

From the very day Pierre had first experienced this feeling at the Sloboda Palace, he had been continuously under its influence, but only now did he find full satisfaction for it. Moreover, at this moment Pierre was sustained in his plan, and prevented from giving it up, by what he had already done in that direction. If he were now to leave Moscow like everyone else, his flight from home, the peasant coat, the pistol, and his announcement to the Rostovs that he would remain in Moscow would all become not merely meaningless but contemptible and ridiculous—and Pierre was very sensitive to that.

Pierre's physical condition, as is always the case, matched his mental state. The unaccustomed coarse food, the vodka he drank during those days, the absence of wine and cigars, his dirty unchanged linen, two almost sleepless nights on a short sofa without bedding—all this kept him in a state of excitement bordering on insanity.

It was two o'clock in the afternoon. The French had already entered Moscow. Pierre knew this, but instead of acting he only thought about his undertaking, going over its smallest details in his mind. In his imagination, he did not clearly picture the striking of the blow or the death of Napoleon, but with extraordinary vividness and melancholy pleasure imagined his own destruction and heroic endurance.

"Yes, alone, for the sake of all, I must do it or die!" he thought. "Yes, I will approach... and then suddenly... with pistol or dagger? But that doesn't matter! 'It is not I but the hand of Providence that punishes you,' I shall say," thought he, imagining what he would say when killing Napoleon. "Well then, take me and execute me!" he went on, speaking to himself and bowing his head with a sad but determined expression.

While Pierre, standing in the middle of the room, was talking to himself this way, the study door opened and on the threshold appeared the figure of Makar Alexeevich, always so timid before but now quite transformed.

His dressing gown was unfastened, his face red and distorted. He was obviously drunk. Seeing Pierre, he was confused at first, but noticing Pierre's own embarrassment, he immediately grew bold and, staggering on his thin legs, advanced into the middle of the room.
"They're frightened," he said in a hoarse, confidential voice. "I say I won't surrender, I say... Am I not right, sir?"
He paused, then suddenly seeing the pistol on the table, seized it with unexpected speed and ran out into the corridor.

Gerasim and the porter, who had followed Makar Alexeevich, stopped him in the vestibule and tried to take the pistol from him. Pierre, coming out into the corridor, looked with pity and revulsion at the half-crazy old man. Makar Alexeevich, straining with effort, held on to the pistol and screamed hoarsely, evidently with some heroic fantasy in his head.
"To arms! Board them! No, you shan't have it!" he yelled.
"That will do, please, that will do. Have the goodness—please, sir, to let go! Please, sir..." pleaded Gerasim, trying carefully to steer Makar Alexeevich by the elbows back to the door.
"Who are you? Bonaparte!..." shouted Makar Alexeevich.
"That's not right, sir. Come to your room, please, and rest. Allow me to have the pistol."
"Get away, you vile slave! Don't touch me! See this?" shouted Makar Alexeevich, brandishing the pistol. "Board them!"
"Grab him!" whispered Gerasim to the porter.
They seized Makar Alexeevich by the arms and dragged him to the door.
The vestibule filled with the discordant sounds of a struggle and a tipsy, hoarse voice.
Suddenly a fresh sound—a piercing feminine scream—rang out from the porch, and the cook came running into the vestibule.
"It's them! Lord have mercy! O Lord, four of them, horsemen!" she cried.
Gerasim and the porter let Makar Alexeevich go, and in the now silent corridor the sound of several hands knocking at the front door could be heard.
